title: Design CI/CD for a Large Frontend Monorepo
followUps: A PR changes one file in a utility library that 40 packages depend on. Walk through exactly what CI computes and runs, and what is served from cache.
Two PRs each pass CI on their own, merge within a minute of each other, and break main together. How does your design prevent that, and what does it cost in merge latency?
A developer's laptop uploads a poisoned artifact to the remote cache. How do you make the cache safe to share between CI and developers, and what makes a cache key correct?
A test fails 2% of the time for reasons unrelated to the change. How does your system detect it, keep it from blocking merges, and get it fixed rather than ignored forever?
The browser extension must go through store review, while the web apps deploy continuously. How does the same pipeline handle both, and how do you roll back each?

interviewer.approach: Strong answers make the dependency graph the centre of the design: compute what a change affects, run only that, and never redo work whose inputs haven't changed. Requirements: PR feedback p50 under 10 minutes, p95 under 20; main always green; required reviews from code owners per package; independent deploys per app; reproducible builds. Estimates: 1,500 PRs/week plus ~5 pushes per PR is ~7,500 pipeline runs/week, ~200/hour at peak; full build+test is ~4 hours of compute (parallelised to 60+ minutes), so running everything costs ~30,000 compute hours/week; with affected-only plus caching, typical PRs touch 5-10% of packages. Pipeline: on push, a planner checks out the merge commit, determines changed files, maps them to packages (plus global inputs such as lockfile, root configs and toolchain versions, which invalidate everything or a defined subset), computes the affected set via reverse dependencies in the package graph, and expands it into a DAG of tasks (lint, typecheck, build, unit test, e2e) per package. Tasks run on an autoscaled runner pool, distributed by DAG order with test sharding by historical duration. Remote cache: content-addressed by a hash of all task inputs (source files, dependency outputs' hashes, toolchain, env vars, command); outputs stored in object storage behind a cache service; CI writes, developers read only (or writes signed and scoped) to prevent poisoning; hermeticity checks to catch undeclared inputs. Merge queue: approved PRs enter a queue; the system tests speculative merges (main + PR1, main + PR1 + PR2, ...) in parallel, merges the passing prefix, and evicts failures, so main is never broken by semantic conflicts. Flaky tests: record results per test over time, auto-retry once and flag if pass-on-retry, quarantine tests above a flakiness threshold (non-blocking but still run and reported), file tickets to the owning team from CODEOWNERS, and track a flake budget. Ownership: CODEOWNERS per package path, required reviewers enforced by the host's branch protection, ownership metadata also used for alert routing. Deploys: each app has a pipeline triggered when main changes affect it; build once, promote the same artifact through staging, canary and production; web apps deploy continuously with feature flags and automatic rollback on error-rate regressions; the extension builds a versioned release candidate on a cadence, submits it to the stores, and uses remote config / staged rollouts since store rollbacks are slow. Observability: CI dashboards for queue time, p50/p95 duration, cache hit rate, flake rate, cost per PR.
hints: Most PRs touch a handful of packages. How do you figure out which other packages a change can break?
If a package's inputs haven't changed since some earlier build anywhere in the company, do you need to build it again? What exactly are its inputs?
Two green PRs can still break main when combined. What would you have to test before merging to rule that out?
What should happen when a test fails, is retried, and passes?
What changes in the pipeline for an app that can't be redeployed instantly?
pitfalls: Running the whole build and test suite on every PR, only with more machines.
Determining affected packages from changed directories alone, ignoring transitive dependents and global inputs such as the lockfile or shared configs.
Cache keys based on branch names, timestamps or a subset of inputs, which serves stale or wrong artifacts.
Letting any machine write to the shared cache without integrity controls.
Testing PRs against an old main and merging without a merge queue, so main breaks on semantic conflicts.
Retrying flaky tests silently until they pass, which hides real failures and never gets them fixed.
Rebuilding artifacts separately for each environment instead of promoting one build.
Treating the browser extension like a web app with instant rollback.
facts: About 300 engineers commit to the monorepo; about 1,500 pull requests are merged per week, and each PR gets about 5 pushes.
The repo has 4 web apps, a browser extension, a design system and about 80 shared libraries, with about 2 million lines of TypeScript.
Running every lint, typecheck, build and test takes about 4 hours of compute; today CI parallelises it to about 65 minutes per run.
A typical PR touches files in 1 to 3 packages, but one core utility library is a dependency of about 70% of packages.
Target: PR checks finish in under 10 minutes at p50 and 20 minutes at p95. main must stay green: a broken main blocks every team's deploys.
About 3% of CI runs currently fail because of flaky tests, and engineers routinely click retry.
Each package has an owning team; changes need approval from an owner of every package touched.
Web apps deploy to production many times a day. The browser extension ships a release every two weeks through the Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge stores, where review can take days.
Engineers also build locally and would like to reuse CI's build outputs.
CI compute budget is fixed; finance has asked for cost per PR to go down, not up.
deepDives: Affected-graph computation: mapping changed files to packages, transitive dependents and global inputs
Content-addressed remote caching: cache keys, hermeticity and protection against poisoning
Merge queue with speculative batches to keep main green
Flaky test detection, quarantine and ownership
Independent deploys: build once, promote, canary, and the extension's store release train
